extracted.intended_audience: citizens, journalists, media executives, financial analysts, scholars, and students
extracted.subtask_description: An annual, cross‑sector assessment of American journalism that evaluates each media sector on multiple dimensions and sets out principles for journalistic quality (verification, transparency, expertise) and metrics for measuring sector health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial content
rubrics_metrics.description: A sense of the editorial content
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each sector the report examines what is actually produced: types of stories, depth, tone, sourcing, and formats (e.g., taped packages vs live interviews). The report includes original content analyses where available to measure these aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience trends
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track measures such as circulation, readership, unique visitors, viewership, demographic composition, growth/decline over time, audience share, and modes of consumption (e.g., satellite, podcasts). Use multiple audience measures (readership vs paid circulation, cume vs average audience) to capture reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic trends
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate advertising revenues, profit margins, revenue breakdowns (retail, general, classified), and how economic pressures influence newsroom decisions and investment. Include year-over-year percentage changes and context (e.g., political advertising spikes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership trends
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine consolidation, cross‑ownership, acquisitions, corporate strategies, and the effects of ownership changes on newsroom resources and editorial decisions. Track major ownership transactions and regulatory impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom investment trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsroom investment trends
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure staffing levels (FTEs), hires/cuts, correspondent counts, foreign bureaus, salary levels, and diversity metrics (minority employment). Assess whether investment is in people (reporters) or primarily in technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public attitudes about that sector
rubrics_metrics.description: Data on public attitudes about that sector
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey data (e.g., Pew) to measure believability, trust, perceived thoroughness, and whether audiences prefer independent/nonpartisan outlets. Track shifts over time and political subgroup differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage scope requirement (nine media sectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report should cover nine media: network television, cable television, newspapers, magazines, the Internet, radio, local TV, ethnic media and the alternative press
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each of these sectors is analyzed on the six core areas (content, audience, economics, ownership, newsroom investment, public attitudes); include original analyses where possible and appendices with data sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism of Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional press model — journalists are concerned first with trying to substantiate facts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize independent verification, multiple and transparent sourcing, and editing processes that allow double‑checking of facts. This is presented as a normative ideal against which other models are judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism of Assertion (anti‑pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is offered with little time or attempt to independently verify its veracity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as a weaker model (common on talk shows, some cable, and parts of the blogosphere) where publishing comes before verification; prone to spreading unsubstantiated claims and manipulation by interest groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism of Affirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: News is gathered with a point of view, whether acknowledged or not, and audiences come to have their preconceptions reinforced
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some outlets intentionally serve audiences seeking affirmation; measurement should note point‑of‑view orientation and its audience consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency / 'Show Me' journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Document the reporting process more openly so that audiences can decide for themselves whether to believe it ('The era of "Trust Me" journalism has passed and the era of "Show Me" journalism has begun')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require disclosure of sourcing, methodology, and reporting steps where possible; transparency serves as inoculation against rapid citizen review and online scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher level of proof / evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Since citizens have a deeper range of information at their fingertips, the level of proof in the press must rise accordingly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect more rigorous fact‑checking, sourcing, use of experts, and documentary evidence in reporting; mere assertion is insufficient when readers can easily verify or dispute claims online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism should enrich its expertise, both on staff and in reporting; the notion of filling newsrooms only with talented generalists may not be enough
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in beat specialists, expert reporters, and training to raise the level of substantive knowledge and analysis conveyed to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring alternative public discussion venues
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations may need to monitor the new alternative means of public discussion as well
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and report on discourse emerging in blogs, forums, and other citizen venues so journalism can referee misinformation and contextualize public conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing quantity and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper stories contain more sources and share more information about those sources (e.g., nearly half contained four or more fully transparent sources)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and reward reporting that cites multiple, clearly identified sources; use counts of sources and transparency labels as proxies for depth and verifiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone measurement (positive/negative/neutral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the tone of coverage (positive, negative, neutral) as part of content analysis
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report tone distributions for major beats (e.g., Iraq coverage) and recognize when coverage tends to be neutral, slightly negative, or otherwise; use tone as one indicator of balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format mix as proxy for thoroughness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of edited/taped packages versus live interviews/standups (e.g., network nightly newscasts: 86% taped packages, 2% live interviews)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mix of story formats to evaluate the opportunity for fact‑checking and crafted reporting (taped packages imply more editing and verification than live segments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness / density of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure thoroughness of reporting by depth, sourcing, and ability to double‑check facts; the report finds all network broadcast news fares better on thoroughness than cable
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess indices of depth (e.g., source counts, investigative follow‑through, edited packages) to compare outlets and formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in online journalism: people vs technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence suggests news organizations have imposed more cutbacks in their Internet operations than in their old media; where investment has come, it is in technology for processing information, not people to gather it
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether online investment is building journalistic capacity (reporters, editors) or only technical tools; favor sustained investment in editorial staffing for quality online journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of algorithms and platform discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The emergence of algorithmic aggregators (e.g., Google News) changes how headlines are selected and how audiences find news
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the influence of technology companies on audience flows, transparency of selection algorithms, and whether editorial judgment is being ceded to automated systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust / believability as outcome metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Use public polls to measure percent who find an outlet 'believable' (e.g., newspapers, networks, cable channels)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track believability across time and by outlet; interpret shifts alongside audience and content measures to assess reputation and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use readership instead of paid circulation as audience metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation problems gave fresh impetus to make readership—rather than paid circulation—the standard measure of audience reach
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer estimates of readers (e.g., Scarborough, NAA readership figures) to raw paid circulation numbers which can be distorted by discounted sales and loopholes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local TV production and platform-sharing metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess local stations by hours of news produced per day, content sharing across platforms, and the percentage of station revenue from newscasts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure production load (hours/day), multi‑platform output (web, radio, cable), and revenue dependency on news (e.g., % of station revenue from newscasts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine topical orientation and ad/page metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate magazine shifts toward topical (current events) coverage and track ad pages and ad dollars
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze editorial mix (national affairs, international, culture, lifestyle) and economic indicators (ad pages, ad dollars, circulation changes) to assess health and editorial direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio reach, format diversification, and compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure radio by overall reach (e.g., percent of Americans reached), emergence of satellite and podcasts, format shifts (Spanish‑language, liberal talk), and salary comparisons
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track platform diversification (satellite, internet), audience use for news/campaign info, and newsroom compensation levels relative to TV; assess staffing plans reported by stations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic and alternative press growth and audience language preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: For ethnic/alternative media track circulation growth, revenue trends, language preferences of audiences (e.g., Latinos' preferences for Spanish TV/radio but English newspapers), and demographic shifts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure both audience and financial growth, generational language shifts, consolidation among ethnic outlets, and how content orientation varies by audience origin.
